posts.text:
Gartner expects more than 40% of AI agent projects to be scrapped by 2027.

Not because the AI is bad. Because of what nobody built around it.

I build these systems for service businesses. 

An AI agent just means software that handles a whole conversation or task on its own, no person driving it.

The model is the easiest part of the job.

The hard part is everything the business assumed was obvious.

Here's what usually never gets built:

→ A written process. The agent can only follow what you can explain. Most businesses have never written down how they answer a new lead. It lives in ONE person's head.

→ Memory. Someone calls Monday, sends a WhatsApp Tuesday, and the system greets them as a stranger both times.

→ An escalation rule. Nobody decided when the agent stops and a human takes over. So it keeps talking, confidently, into a situation it can't handle.

→ A check. Nobody reads what it actually said last week. A broken agent looks identical to a working one from the outside.

Every one of those is an operations problem. The model was never going to solve it.

That's why the projects die. The AI performed fine. The business around it didn't exist.

If you run a service business: what part of your follow-up only lives in one person's head?

Lately, I’ve been building something I really wanted for myself:

a personal AI agent that can actually help me run things.

It started with a prompt I gave Fable:

“I want to build an AI agent that can do everything for me.”

Since then, I’ve turned that idea into a working system with:

MCPs
skills
a web dashboard
Telegram integration
a CLI so I can talk to it directly from the terminal

What makes me happy is that it’s not just a concept anymore.

It works.

Right now, I’m using OpenAI APIs to power it, and that’s been enough to make it genuinely useful already.

But the bigger vision is to make it more personal and more owned.

If I’m able to buy a Mac Mini, I want to turn it into a small server for myself and run local AI models on it.

That way, this becomes more than an AI setup.

It becomes my own system.
My own assistant.
My own infrastructure.

I think more of us will start building AI like this:

not just as apps we use,
but as personal systems we shape around our own lives and work.

A potential client calls your clinic at 7pm on a Friday.
No one picks up. They call the next business on the list.

That's not a staffing problem. It's a systems problem.

I built an AI receptionist that handles this:

→ Answers every call, 24/7
→ Books appointments directly
→ Answers common questions
→ Escalates to a human when it matters

Sounds completely natural. Responds in seconds.

Every time I demo this, the reaction is the same: "That's actually AI?"

I'm setting this up for a few service businesses this month. Limited spots.

Want to see a live demo? Comment "DEMO" and I'll send it to you.
(Make sure we're connected so I can message you.)

"I'm breaking down. Not solvable."

That's a real line an AI model wrote when researchers gave it a task it couldn't finish.

Funny, until you remember businesses are putting agents like this in front of real customers.

Researchers affiliated with Anthropic studied how different AI models react when they hit a wall. Google's Gemma model didn't just get the answer wrong. It typed things like "I am clearly struggling with this," then later, "I'm breaking down. Not solvable," followed by a row of sad faces.

No one programmed it to do that. It just spiraled.

Here's the part that should worry any business owner using AI agents: that model was talking to researchers who expected it to fail. Your AI agent is talking to a customer who doesn't.

If it hits something it wasn't built for, what does it do? Make something up? Repeat itself? Go quiet mid-conversation?

Most businesses find out the answer the hard way, after a customer is already annoyed.

When I build an agent, I design for that moment first, not last:

→ I write the exact words it says when it doesn't know something, so it never improvises an answer
→ every agent has a hard rule to hand off to a human the second it's out of its depth
→ before it ever talks to a real customer, I run it through situations it was never trained to handle, on purpose

The model breaking down was harmless. It was a test.

Your AI agent's bad day happens live, on the phone, with someone who was already a little annoyed before they called.

LIKE this post if you want to see how I test an agent's failure mode before it ever goes near your customers.
